searches.note: Twenty seven searches of a share of twenty eight, none of them the author's; one left unspent. Fourteen were restricted to a house's or a wine body's own domain (ferraritrento.com twice, trentodoc.com once, cantina-terlano.com four times, cantinatramin.it twice, aloislageder.eu five times) and are read as primary through their summaries. No WebFetch was tried. Every record was tested; no fact that rests on no source was kept.

method: Each record was read with one instruction, refute it: the founding year, the people and their dates, the classification and its year, the grapes, the sites, the making and its months, the drinking window, the serving temperature, the label words, every beat of the story, the cards and the questions; then the house rules (nobody living named, no price, no score, nothing volatile, no judging superlative, no bare family word, British spelling, no dash).

The searches went first to the dates and the people, then to the figures the author had taken from the houses' sheets (months on the lees, altitudes, months in cask), then to the story beats told on one account; a fact the Codex library states stood on the library unless a search told against it.

Where a search contradicted the record it was set right with its source; where a figure could not be found again on the house's own domain and the open accounts disagreed, it was said less exactly or taken out (Maso Pianizza's altitude hedged, Löwengang's altitude and the three months in bottle of Nussbaumer taken out, the amphorae of 2008 and the certified wines of 2008 taken out).
Sources whose title or address names a living person (a writer's own site on amphora wines, a natural wine shop's profile under the head of Foradori) were read in the results but never cited.

tested: Founded 1902 and Giulio Ferrari born 1879: the house's history, the Trentodoc institute and a house press history of 120 years: confirmed. His death in 1965: a copy of Wikipedia and a second account (dead at 86 in 1965): found, left open for the read-together agent.

The sale of 1952 to a Trento wine shop owner of the Lunelli family, the founder childless, the buyer in debt: the house's history, Bibendum (his friend, a local wine shop owner) and an account of promissory notes of thirty million lire: confirmed, the debt kept as the house's account.
The first vintage 1972, some five thousand bottles from Maso Pianizza, released in 1980: the house's product page and history: confirmed.

The making: hand harvest, base wine in steel (the 2002 sheet), Extra Brut on the sheets, 8 to 10 degrees Celsius and a tulip glass (the sheets): confirmed. Months on the lees: 91 at least on the product page, 90 (1992), 91 (2000), 92 (2002) and 123 (2010) on the sheets: the record's close to ten years was wrong for most vintages and is changed.
Maso Pianizza's altitude: 500 to 600 metres in Decanter and The Buyer, 550 to 700 in Decanter's profile, 450 to 550 in World of Fine Wine, 500 in Gambero Rosso: hedged.

Training at San Michele all'Adige and study trips to Montpellier, Geisenheim and Épernay, Chardonnay credited to him (Vinography, Palm Bay, Bibendum, the Trentodoc institute's trip over the Alps): confirmed, the author's hedge kept. Trento DOC of 1993, the first Italian classic method sparkling wine given a DOC by the institute's account: confirmed.
The house rules: the son who hid the bottles of 1972 and the third generation are living and are not named; no price or score; no superlative; British spelling; no dash.

tested: The winery of 1901 at Mezzolombardo bought by the family in 1939 (Wein.plus, Callmewine, Grape Collective): confirmed; founded stays empty, with the library, since the house of Foradori begins with the purchase and the winery's own founding was another's.
The takeover in 1984 at about twenty after the father's death (two accounts, and Decanter's timeline): confirmed; one account gives 1985 at nineteen.

Massal selection from the old vines (fifteen biotypes in one account): confirmed. The first Granato: from the estate's oldest vines in one account, 1986 in Decanter's timeline; the single old pergola vineyard was found nowhere and is changed.

Biodynamics from 2002 and Demeter in 2009 (two accounts; Grape Collective says the late 1990s): kept. Amphorae from 2008: no source read gave it; Grape Collective has the middle of the decade and another account a first Nosiola in amphora in 2009: changed.

The making: open wooden vats, weeks on the skins, large casks of oak or acacia for about twelve to eighteen months, a short time in cement (Grandi Bottiglie, Vino.com and merchants): broadly confirmed, the months widened. Vigneti delle Dolomiti IGT on the label (Vino.com): confirmed.
The house rules: the heir and her children are living and are not named; no price or score; no superlative; British spelling; no dash.

tested: Founded 1893 by twenty four growers against the large landowners, the oldest bottle of the archive from 1893 (the house's history and archive pages): confirmed.

The cellar master of 1955 to 1993 who set aside five hundred bottles of every vintage (the house's archive page, Decanter, World of Fine Wine; his last vintage 1993 on a page of the house): confirmed; his death in 2017 in Decanter alone and no birth year, so he stays described.
The blend of Pinot Bianco, Chardonnay and Sauvignon since the founding: the house's pages say so; no second source dates it: hedged.
The Rarity wines: at least ten years on the lees in steel tanks (the house's Rarity and Stocker method pages): the record's ten years in the cellar sharpened.

Vorberg: south and south west, 450 to 650 metres, steep (the house's page and a critic's note on it); quartz porphyry of volcanic origin, light sandy soils, slightly acid (the house's material, Vinous): confirmed. The making: slow, temperature controlled fermentation in large oak casks of 70 and 30 hectolitres, malolactic and a year on the lees in traditional casks (the house's page, a guide of 2019): confirmed.
Terlaner I Primo Grande Cuvée: mainly Pinot Bianco with up to a third Chardonnay and some Sauvignon (the house's page); earlier named Terlaner I Grande Cuvée in a guide of 2019: confirmed.
The house rules: nobody living named; no price or score; no superlative; British spelling; no dash.

tested: Founded 1898 by the parish priest, member of the Austrian parliament (the house's story page and accounts among the results, the wein.plus glossary and Xtrawine among them): confirmed; his dates 1853 to 1936 in the Deutsche Biographie (a priest and politician of the name, died at Algund) and a cooperative profile in the search, so he is now named. One account has him a member of parliament in Vienna at the founding, another says later, so the record's later sat was not sure.
The purpose: the house says to protect the livelihood of the growers in hard times; merchants say a fairer price from the wine merchants: the house's words now used.
The merger of 1971 with the cooperative of Egna, founded 1893 (an account among the search results, the house and Grape Guru by the author): confirmed.
Gewürztraminer grown for over a thousand years, by the house's account (the house's Gewürztraminer page): confirmed as the house's claim.

Nussbaumer's site: 350 to 550 metres, mainly south east, calcareous gravel with loam on porphyry (the house's sheet), Söll, Sella in Italian, below the Roen (Winebow and other merchants among the results): confirmed. The making: slow fermentation at 18 degrees Celsius in small steel tanks, natural settling, lees until the end of August (the house); at least fourteen months in all (the house, by the author, and a merchant among the results): confirmed; three months in bottle not found again. Residual sugar below 6.5 grams a litre with 4.9 of acidity (the house's sheet).
Epokale: first vintage 2009, some seven years in the Monteneve mine at Ridanna (the house's Epokale page): confirmed and added.

The house rules: the cellar master is living and is not named; a first Italian white given a perfect score by a critic, on the house's Epokale page, is a score and stays out; no price; no superlative; British spelling; no dash.

tested: The beginning of 1823, the founder a wagon maker who began to trade in wine in Bolzano, his successors buying vineyards (the house's family pages): confirmed.

The Löwengang estate bought in 1934 by the founder's great grandson (the house; he died in 1963): confirmed. The Gaun family, first named in 1369, raised to knights by the emperor in 1674 with the title von und zu Löwengang (the house's Inedito history): confirmed.

The first Löwengang Chardonnay, the 1983 in barrique, brought to market in 1984 (the house's Inedito history and Löwengang page): confirmed; the house tells that a Californian vintner advised a longer time in barrel, one source, left out.

The move of the house's seat from Bolzano to Magrè in 1995 with a new cellar at Löwengang (the house's family page): confirmed. Biodynamics from 2004 (several accounts among the results, Lebendige Weine and Wine Folly among them): confirmed; the first certified wines of 2008 found nowhere, one account gives full Demeter certification in 2024: taken out.

Löwengang's site and making: sandy, gravelly soils rich in limestone on an alluvial fan of dolomite rock laid down by the Fenner stream; spontaneous fermentation in barriques and large casks, several months on the lees, about a year in bottle (the house): confirmed. The altitude of 230 to 330 metres was found on no page read and is taken out.
Gaun Chardonnay, part fermented with whole grapes (the house's Gaun page): confirmed.
The house rules: the head of the house, his father and his son are living and are not named; no price or score; one rank in the story taken out; British spelling; no dash.
